title: Visas, the One-Year Rule and Staying Legal in Georgia
excerpt: Citizens of 94 countries can stay a full year with no visa — but since January 2026 you need travel insurance to get in at all, since October 2025 an overstay carries an entry ban as well as a fine, and since March 2026 even a self-employed foreigner needs permission to work. The annual visa run still works for most people and is no longer a sure thing.
bodyHtml:
One year, no visa — for most of us

Since 1 January 2026 every tourist entering Georgia must carry valid health and accident insurance covering the whole stay, with cover of at least GEL 30,000. Paper or screen, Georgian or English, a foreign insurer is fine, and holders of a Georgian residence permit are exempt — but without it you can be refused at the border, so buy it before you fly. With that done, Georgia runs one of the loosest entry regimes in the region. Government Ordinance No. 255 of 5 June 2015, still amended as recently as February 2026, lists the countries whose citizens enter without a visa, and for the great majority — 94 countries and territories — the allowance is 'one full year' from each entry. A handful get less: 90 days for Chile, Fiji, North Macedonia, Paraguay, Peru and Uruguay, 45 for Iran, 30 for China, Hong Kong and Macau. Check your own passport on geoconsul.gov.ge rather than trusting a count. The list covers every EU state, the UK, Norway, Iceland, Switzerland, the USA, Canada, Mexico, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Thailand, Israel, the Gulf states, Türkiye, Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Armenia, Kazakhstan and the Central Asian republics. A separate rule lets holders of a valid visa or residence permit from the EU/EFTA, the USA, the UK, Canada, Australia, Japan, South Korea, Israel, New Zealand or a Gulf state enter for up to 90 days in any 180, so long as that document is valid on arrival.

Ordinary passport holders from India, Pakistan, Nigeria, the Philippines, Vietnam and Egypt need a visa; Chinese citizens get 30 days visa-free. Short-stay applicants use the e-visa portal (evisa.gov.ge). The tourism board says a decision on a visa 'is made within 5 to 30 calendar days, depending on the visa category', so don't book flights first.

The visa run — and why it is no longer a sure thing

Because the year runs from each entry, people have long treated Georgia as a place you can live indefinitely by crossing to Armenia or Türkiye once a year and coming straight back. That still works for most people. It has not been guaranteed since 2022. Border police can refuse entry citing 'other cases envisaged by Georgian legislation' with no further explanation, and the refusals have grown: JAMnews has reported Russians increasingly deported or turned back when trying to reset their stay; the Committee to Protect Journalists counts at least sixteen foreign journalists denied entry since 2022, six of them European in recent months; Kazakhstan has asked Tbilisi to explain refusals of its citizens, and France and Poland issued travel advisories in May 2025. Unpaid fines, a political profile or a passport full of Georgian stamps and no visible income can all be enough.

The overstay trap. Under amendments passed in June 2025 and in force from autumn 2025, overstaying is no longer a fine you pay on the way out. Up to three months over brings an entry ban of six months; three months to a year, two years; over a year, three years — each with a fine that scales, and an unpaid fine blocks any future visa or entry. A register of illegally present foreigners went live on 1 October 2025, and appealing a refusal or deportation no longer suspends it. Count your days from the entry stamp, not from memory.

When you want more than a stamp: the residence permit

A temporary residence permit is what turns you from a tourist into a resident: it gives you a residence card with an 11-digit personal number, the key to banking, a registered lease, an Individual Entrepreneur registration and most online government services. The main routes on the Public Service Development Agency's list: work (employed or running a business; income at least five times the subsistence minimum, and from 1 March 2026 a formal work authorisation must come first, with a transition period to 1 January 2027); study at an accredited institution; family reunification with a permit holder; short-term/property — title to non-agricultural real estate worth at least USD 150,000 by accredited valuation, raised from USD 100,000 on 1 March 2026, with the old figure kept for anyone whose ownership was registered before that date, even if they apply later; investment from USD 300,000 with turnover conditions; and a new IT permit (two years' experience, USD 25,000 annual income, three-year validity renewable to twelve). Check every threshold at sda.gov.ge before you buy or sign anything — three of them changed in 2025–26.

Apply while you are still legally in the country — the agency asks for the application 40 days before your lawful stay runs out — at any Public Service Hall (the 'Justice House' in Tbilisi and the regional cities), a territorial office, or online at services.sda.gov.ge. Standard processing is 30 days, with paid 20- and 10-day options. Police clearance certificates from home are increasingly requested. Once the permit is granted, collect the residence card, then register your address within one month — it is free, but needs the property owner's written consent.

The right to work, new since March 2026

This is the change that catches people out, because it undoes the thing Georgia was famous for. A government resolution adopted on 20 February 2026 and in force from 1 March 2026 created a work-authorisation regime where none had existed: being in the country lawfully — on the visa-free year, on any stamp — no longer carries the right to work or to run a business. The right to work is now a separate permission, granted through the State Employment Support Agency, and it applies whether you are on a local payroll, doing paid work here, working remotely for a Georgian employer, or self-employed.

It arrived in stages: employees from 1 March 2026, the self-employed — freelancers and Individual Entrepreneurs included — from 1 May 2026, and anyone already registered as a labour immigrant and active on 1 March has until 1 January 2027. That last date is the one most of us are actually under, and it is close. Working without the authorisation carries a GEL 2,000 fine that can land on the employer, the employee or the self-employed person alike; a second offence doubles it, a third triples it.

It also reorders the nomad playbook. The 1% Small Business Status below is no longer the first move: a foreign national needs the authorisation active before earning the revenue the 1% is meant to tax, so the old sequence — register the Individual Entrepreneur, start invoicing, sort the paperwork afterwards — is now backwards, and the wrong order is what the fine is for. Two changes from March 2026 are worth knowing before you file: Small Business Status now takes effect on the date you request it rather than the first of the following month, and a monthly declaration is compulsory even in a month with no turnover — a missed filing is an offence now, where it used to pass as a zero return. One case the sources do not settle is the member employed by a foreign company who simply lives here: the rule is written around local employers and the self-employed, and that gap is worth an hour of an accountant's time rather than an assumption in either direction.

The tax line at 183 days

Spend 183 days or more in Georgia in any continuous twelve-month period ending in the tax year and you are a Georgian tax resident. Georgia taxes individuals territorially — genuinely foreign-source income (dividends, interest, gains on assets abroad) is generally untaxed — but 'foreign' is about where the work happens, not where the money lands: a freelancer sitting in Vake billing a client in Berlin is earning Georgian-source income. That is why nomads register as an Individual Entrepreneur with Small Business Status at the Revenue Service (rs.ge): 1% of turnover up to GEL 500,000 a year, 3% on anything above, monthly declarations, and the status lapses after two years over the cap. Lawyers, doctors, architects, auditors and consultants are excluded. Since 2026 there is a gate in front of it: the work authorisation above has to be active first, and the status now takes effect from the day you file for it rather than later. Take the 2026 rules to an accountant — the rs.ge pages still carry older figures.

The neighbours who arrived in 2022

Say it plainly: since February 2022 Georgia has absorbed a large Russian-speaking arrival. The 2024 census counted 37,715 Russian citizens among 133,857 foreign citizens, alongside 11,542 Ukrainians (1,631 in 2014) and 4,473 Belarusians (101); ethnic Russians numbered 42,525, up from 26,453 in 2014; The Insider puts the three groups at about 108,000 by 2026. Tbilisi rents doubled year-on-year in May 2022. Many Georgians hold the Russian state, not its émigrés, responsible for the occupied 20% of their country — but the welcome is cooler than the visa regime suggests, and the border refusals above fall hardest on exactly this group.
